child_mission: Become a Number Investigator! Use place groups to solve read and count whole numbers tasks and explain how you checked.
evidence_instructions: Keep the read and count whole numbers answers, two worked decisions, checking note, reflection and written quiz responses.
extension: Choose a new number below 100,000. Represent it in words and two partitions, then explain how it compares with 64,518.
guided_practice:
WE DO: Prepare a second record using 60,426.
1. Label the columns and insert the digits. Read it before comparing with “sixty thousand four hundred and twenty-six”.
2. Find the hundreds digit and its contribution. Compare after your attempt: 400.
3. Partition it. Check against 60,000 + 400 + 20 + 6, then add those terms back.
4. Compare 60,426 with 64,518; name the first unequal place rather than choosing by the final digit.
5. Make one different partition by setting aside a hundred. Check: 60,326 + 100.
6. Explain one check you used. If you made an error, repair only the mismatched place and read the result again.
You can draw the chart or describe it in text. The explanation matters more than decorative layout.
independent_task:
YOU DO: Read and count whole numbers record (about 20 minutes).
Use these numbers: 64,721; 60,536; 64,506; 60,406.
1. Say what each part of the task asks before answering: numeral, words, place value, partition or order.
2. Write each numeral in words and give the next two counts by one. Explain what happens at the range boundary.
3. Show working for at least two decisions with a labelled chart, equation or comparison reason.
4. Check those decisions by rebuilding a total, reading words back or comparing neighbouring values.
5. Explain one improvement or one check that confirmed a correct answer.
Work on paper or in the big box. If using paper, type the answers and a clear working summary. Check: correct range and places; zeroes preserved; complete requested representations; a specific reason and a check. An upload is optional.
learning_intention: We are learning to read and count whole numbers within the range to 100,000.
materials: Everything you need to read is included in this lesson
offline_alternative: Copy the four task numbers and draw place columns on paper. Complete the read and count whole numbers record and check it, then type your evidence later.

subject: Number and Algebra
success_criteria: I can read a numeral through its place groups.
I can match a digit to its value.
I can show a correct partition or comparison.
I can check an answer and explain my reason.

check.explanation: Ten groups of one hundred contain one thousand units. Regrouping changes the grouping, not the total.
options: They become ten ones
They become one thousand
They become one hundred
They disappear from the count
check.question: What happens when ten hundreds are grouped together?

teach_steps.example:
I DO:
64,518 has 8 ones at the right. The next column records tens, then hundreds, then thousands, then ten thousands. I use columns instead of counting 64,518 individual cards.

YOU TRY:
How many tens make one hundred? Use equal bundles before checking.

CHECK:
Ten tens make one hundred because ten groups of ten contain a hundred units. It is not one ten with a different name.
teach_steps.explain:
**A whole number counts complete units.**
An item count such as a number of cards uses whole units, not parts of one card. Large counts are organised into equal groups so we do not have to count every item again.

**Each place is ten times the place to its right.**
Ten ones make a ten. Ten tens make a hundred. Ten hundreds make a thousand. Ten thousands make a ten thousand. Picture bundling ten small groups into one larger group. The written places record how many of each group there are.

**Keep the range in view.**
Today we read whole numbers up to 100,000. A new place appears when every lower place reaches nine and one more unit is added. This is a change in grouping, not a new kind of number.

Start at the ones place on the right. Name each column before reading its digit; a digit’s shape alone does not tell its value.
teach_steps.notice: Read from the right to identify places, then from the left to say the whole number.
teach_steps.title: Build the number from equal groups

check.explanation: Sixty-four thousand five hundred and eighteen matches the thousands part and the remaining hundreds, tens and ones. The other readings change a digit’s value.
options: sixty-four thousand six hundred and eighteen
sixty-four thousand four hundred and eighteen
sixty-four thousand five hundred and eighteen
sixty-four thousand five hundred and twenty-eight
check.question: Which words correctly read 64,518?

teach_steps.example:
I DO:
64,518 = 60,000 + 4,000 + 500 + 10 + 8.
Words: sixty-four thousand five hundred and eighteen.
I match each spoken group with its column, then read the whole count once.

YOU TRY:
Read 60,426 using the columns. Try before comparing.

CHECK:
It is sixty thousand four hundred and twenty-six. The zero column contributes no groups of that size, but still holds its place.
teach_steps.explain:
**Digit and value are different.**
A digit is a written symbol from zero to nine. Its value depends on the place. A four in the hundreds column means four hundreds; in the ones column it means four ones.

**Read a useful chunk.**
In 64,518, separate the thousands part from the final three digits. Read the thousands part, then the hundreds, tens and ones that follow. A space or comma can help group digits; it does not mean a decimal point.

**Say the number in words.**
Our model is “sixty-four thousand five hundred and eighteen”. Say the number, point to each matching part and check that you did not turn a digit into the wrong-sized group.

The same method works with fewer or more non-zero places. The number of digits gives a starting clue, but the position of each digit settles its value.
teach_steps.notice: Do not read every digit as a separate number name when the task asks for the whole number.
teach_steps.title: Read the digits through their places

check.explanation: The zero marks an empty place and keeps later digits in their intended columns. Removing it changes those positions.
options: It makes all other digits worthless
It means the whole count is zero
It is only decoration
It preserves the positions of the other digits
check.question: Why keep an internal zero when writing a whole number?

teach_steps.example:
I DO:
60,426 = 60,000 + 400 + 20 + 6.
I preserve its zero column in the numeral. Omitting a zero term from the sum does not allow me to omit the place from the numeral.

YOU TRY:
Write “sixty thousand four hundred and twenty-six” from its place groups, then read your result back.

CHECK:
The numeral is 60,426. Compare every column, not just the digits you pronounced.
teach_steps.explain:
**Zero can hold an empty column.**
It says there are no groups of that size. It is still important because it keeps the other digits in their intended places. Deleting an internal zero shifts later digits and changes the value.

**Compare two readings.**
Read 60,426 in the chart. Identify the zero column before saying the complete number. It does not make the entire count zero. It only marks an empty place within the count.

**Write from words with the same care.**
Write the needed place columns first. Fill each stated group, then use zero for a column with no group. Check the result by reading it back. This is safer than writing only the non-zero digits you hear.

When using expanded form, you can omit a zero term because it adds nothing. When writing the numeral, preserve the column itself.
teach_steps.notice: A place holder is part of the numeral’s structure. Empty is not the same as missing.
teach_steps.title: Keep zero as a place holder

check.explanation: 100,000 is one greater than 99,999; the completed lower groups regroup into the next place.
check.question: What comes immediately after 99,999 when counting by one?

teach_steps.example:
I DO:
99,998, 99,999, 100,000.
I bundle the completed lower groups. Backwards: 100,000, 99,999, 99,998.

YOU TRY:
What is one more than 64,518? Which column changes?

CHECK:
It is 64,519. Only the final ones digit changes here because no lower group is completed. A boundary can change more columns, but not every counting step does.
teach_steps.explain:
**One more can change several digits.**
When the ones reach nine, the next unit completes a ten. When every lower column reaches nine, the next unit completes the next larger group. Think about bundling rather than simply putting an extra digit at the end.

**Use a known boundary.**
After 99,999 comes 100,000. The lower nines regroup into one new leading unit. The zeroes show that no leftover smaller groups remain. The count increases by one, not by a whole extra set of unrelated digits.

**Check in both directions.**
Count one forward and one back. If the previous number returns, the step fits. Explain the changed groups so you know why the written change happened.

When a task asks you to count, check its step size too. Counting by one and counting by ten are different jobs; do not silently change the step.
teach_steps.notice: Count the units and explain regrouping. Attaching a zero would multiply a number by ten, not add one.
teach_steps.title: Cross a counting boundary and check

title: Year 4: Read and count whole numbers
worked_example:
I DO: Complete a connected read and count whole numbers record.
Target numeral: 64,518. Words: sixty-four thousand five hundred and eighteen.
Standard partition: 60,000 + 4,000 + 500 + 10 + 8.
Hundreds digit: 5; value: 500.
Another partition: 64,418 + 100 = 64,518.
Comparison: 64,518 > 60,426. I compare matching places from the left; the first unequal place decides. The difference is 4,092.
Ascending set: 60,426, 64,518, 64,618.

WHY THE REPRESENTATIONS AGREE
The written numeral, words and expanded sum describe the same place groups. The non-standard partition also returns the same total. Comparing uses those group values, not only the shape of a single digit.

COMMON MISTAKE AND FIX
Writing the hundreds digit’s value as 5 loses its unit size. I change the value label to 500. Another possible error is deleting the zero in 60,426; I keep its column and reread the whole count.

CHECK
I rebuild the numeral from its non-zero terms and read the comparison in both directions. If a check disagrees, I revisit the relevant column before changing unrelated digits.
